topic.label: EEG & Signal Methods
topic.description: EEG signal processing, sleep staging, neural time series, modeling, and practical analysis methods.

papers.title: Lifespan Trajectories of Resting State Bipolar EEG Power
papers.abstract: Normative trajectories of resting state bipolar EEG power over the lifespan were derived from a sample of 5781 participants from the Collaborative Study on the Genetics of Alcoholism (COGA), a large multi site study, using 12,906 observations from ages 12 through 70. Trajectories were analyzed using the means, variances, and correlations of data in seven frequency bands (from low theta to high beta) and 24 bipolar channels obtained from 17 electrodes of the 10-20 system. In order to make the study more useful for understanding EEG in the general population, only subjects never having an alcohol use disorder (AUD) diagnosis were included in the study. Bipolar EEG data is derived from the differencing of the signals in adjacent electrodes, either in a lateral (left-right) or sagittal (anterior-posterior) orientation; each difference is called a channel. The power values for the individual observations were calculated by standard Fourier transform based methods. In all cases there are sharp decreases in EEG power from ages 12 to the early 20s after which there are number of divergent patterns: general increases in the beta frequencies, and mixed patterns of increase and subsequent decrease in the theta and alpha frequencies. In these characteristics the lifespan trajectories presented here are similar to the monopolar trajectories described in our previous study \citet{Cho2026}. Sagittal and lateral bipolar trajectories are similar within each sex and between sexes; the primary difference is the much lower degree of regional difference in the sagittal trajectories as compared to the lateral trajectories. The pairwise inter-frequency (within channel) correlation trajectories between the four theta and alpha frequency bands and the four high alpha and beta frequency bands at each channel show striking sex differences unlike the corresponding monopolar correlations. There are a number of features in the bipolar power trajectories that suggest that the differencing procedure reduces not only local phase synchrony, but also effects of global and regional phase synchrony present in the monopolar data from which the bipolar signals are derived. The inter-frequency correlations at the individual channels are much higher in the bipolar data than the monopolar data, suggesting that global and regional phase synchrony components retained in the monopolar data have greater frequency specificity than the more purely local components in the bipolar data. Further analyses to examine many other features of the data will be undertaken in our subsequent work.

ai.reason: Large normative EEG dataset with spectral power analyses across human lifespan; highly relevant for signal normalization, spectral methods, and longitudinal modeling, with transferable insights for animal sleep research.
ai.summary: Derived normative lifespan trajectories of resting-state bipolar EEG power from 12,906 observations (ages 12–70) in 5,781 alcohol-use-disorder-free COGA participants across seven frequency bands and 24 channels. Found sharp power decreases from ages 12 to early 20s, followed by beta increases and mixed theta/alpha patterns, with sagittal and lateral trajectories similar within and between sexes but bipolar inter-frequency correlations showing striking sex differences.

papers.title: Secondary exploratory discrete wavelet analysis of the electroretinogram in adults with ADHD.
papers.abstract: Conventional electroretinographic (ERG) analyses identified sex-specific retinal differences in adults with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). We applied the discrete wavelet transform (DWT) to the same recordings to characterize multiscale time-frequency features. ERGs from 25 adults with ADHD and 25 age- and sex-matched controls (16 female and 9 male pairs) were analyzed at seven flash intensities. Six DWT descriptors were extracted, and global scores averaged across intensities. Paired comparisons used false-discovery-rate correction. Secondary analyses examined intensity, sex, eyes, inter-eye agreement, within-session repeatability, current medication status, and exploratory classification. Global 40a and 20b values were lower in ADHD (Cohen's dz. = -0.63 and - 0.60; FDR q = 0.020 for both). Differences increased with flash intensity and had the same direction in female and male pairs and both eyes, without significant group × sex or group × eye interactions. Findings were stable across participant- and intensity based sensitivity analyses. Inter-eye ICC(A,1) was 0.750 for 40a and 0.865 for 20b; bilateral within-session ICC(A,1) values ranged from 0.839 to 0.981. Reductions were also present among the eight ADHD participants reporting no current ADHD medication use (dz = -0.74 and - 0.84). Exploratory leave-one-pair-out AUCs ranged from 0.653 to 0.731. DWT analysis identified lower 40a and 20b values as candidate retinal time-frequency features of ADHD. Their consistency across sensitivity analyses, sexes, eyes, medication strata, and repeated measurements supports prospective evaluation in independent, clinically characterized cohorts.

ai.topic: Wavelet Analysis of ERG in ADHD
ai.reason: Directly applies discrete wavelet time-frequency analysis to neural/physiological signals, offering a lightweight and transferable method for EEG/EMG/ACC and artifact characterization, though not sleep-specific.
ai.summary: Applied discrete wavelet transform (DWT) to electroretinogram (ERG) recordings from 25 adults with ADHD and 25 matched controls across seven flash intensities to extract multiscale time-frequency descriptors. Found lower global 40a and 20b DWT values in ADHD (dz = -0.63 and -0.60; FDR q = 0.020), consistent across sexes, eyes, medication strata, and sensitivity analyses, with exploratory classification AUCs of 0.653–0.731.

papers.title: Polysomnographic Sleep in Idiopathic Nightmares: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
papers.abstract: This study conducted a systematic evaluation of polysomnographic differences between individuals with nightmares and healthy controls. Electronic searches of All EBM databases, EMBASE, Web of Science, and MEDLINE identified 14 eligible case-control studies; seven studies involving 112 individuals with nightmares and 112 controls were included in meta-analysis. The meta-analysis of sleep macro-architecture (such as total sleep time, wake after sleep onset, and sleep stage percentages) revealed no significant differences between individuals with nightmares and healthy controls. Furthermore, the limited available data regarding sleep micro-architecture (cyclic alternating patterns (CAP) and power spectral analysis (PSA)) and autonomic measures (heart rate and heart rate variability) in studies not subjected to meta-analysis makes it difficult to draw confident conclusions. Our meta-analysis revealed no significant differences in sleep macro-architecture. This finding highlights the importance of investigating sleep micro-architecture (such as CAP and PSA), which may be relevant to the physiology of nightmares. However, these findings should be interpreted cautiously and validated in future studies because of the limited available data.

ai.reason: Systematic review and meta-analysis of polysomnographic sleep macro/micro-architecture in nightmares; directly relevant to sleep staging and PSG methodology, though clinical rather than computational.
ai.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis of polysomnographic differences between individuals with idiopathic nightmares and healthy controls, including 14 case-control studies with 7 studies (112 cases, 112 controls) in the meta-analysis. Found no significant differences in sleep macro-architecture (total sleep time, wake after sleep onset, sleep stage percentages), while limited micro-architecture and autonomic data precluded confident conclusions.

papers.title: A generalized scaling law reveals synchrony-driven reorganization of brain dynamics across human lifespan.
papers.abstract: Ecological systems obey universal scaling laws such as Taylor's law, which links population variance to the sample mean. Whether other complex systems with integrated and segregated network topology, the human brain, in particular, follow analogous scaling laws, and how these laws behave under synchronized neural activity, remains unknown. To address this question, our initial attempt to implement the Taylor's law, has been hindered because neural signals at all measurement scales contain both positive and negative values, whereas Taylor's law was restricted to non-negative ecological data [1]. To circumvent this limitation, we extend spatial Taylor's law by replacing the sample mean with the root-mean-square (RMS) of the measurements, and apply this generalized law to detrended multivariate neural time series. The detrending operation has been performed as a necessary step to remove the trends and temporal mean from the data. Within this framework, we address our next question how synchronous or coordinated activity of the brain network influences the scaling law. We quantify synchrony using a dedicated metric of functional coordination and show analytically, and via numerical simulations using multivariate Poisson, negative binomial, uniform and gamma distributions, that the scaling exponent is inversely related to synchrony. Applying this approach to human fMRI data from three large cohorts (N = 840, ages 18-88 years) reveals distinct age-related trajectories of the scaling exponent, with healthy aging characterized by a substantial synchrony-induced reduction in this exponent. The synchrony-scaling relationship remains stable during resting-state activity but progressively shifts during naturalistic tasks across the lifespan, and is pronounced in limbic, subcortical, and cerebellar subnetworks, indicating preservation at subnetwork levels. Finally, individuals with ADHD exhibit altered synchrony-scaling coupling, highlighting the potential clinical and translational utility of this generalized scaling metric.

ai.topic: Generalized scaling law for brain dynamics across lifespan
ai.reason: Provides a general analytical scaling framework for multivariate neural time series and synchrony, potentially transferable to EEG analysis and sleep-state dynamics.
ai.summary: The authors generalized Taylor's law to neural data by replacing the sample mean with the root mean square and applied it to detrended multivariate fMRI time series, showing analytically and in simulations that the scaling exponent is inversely related to synchrony. In three large human cohorts (N=840, ages 18–88), the scaling exponent showed age-related trajectories and synchrony-induced reduction, with altered synchrony-scaling coupling in ADHD.

papers.title: Distinct EEG microstate signatures across different pain types
papers.abstract: Pain is associated with dynamic brain reorganization. Electroencephalographic microstates can characterize transient large-scale brain states, yet findings across pain studies are inconsistent. Two features may contribute: conditions have been studied in isolation, and analytical pipelines vary widely. We applied a harmonized analysis pipeline across three pain conditions: capsaicininduced pain, assessed within participants against a pain-free baseline, and non-chronic and chronic back pain, each compared with matched controls. Using a five-minute resting-state electroencephalographic recordings we examined microstate topography, temporal expression and transition probabilities, and directly compared pain related differences across pain states. We identified five microstates (A-E), corresponding to auditory, visual, salience, and attentional networks. Capsaicin pain showed increased expression of microstate C and reduced expression of microstates A, D and E. Transitions were redistributed towards microstate C, indicating a shift toward salience-related processing at the expense of sensory and attentional dynamics. In clinical back pain, effects were smaller and diverged by pain type: non-chronic back pain showed lower microstate C occurrence, opposite in direction to the capsaicin effect, whereas chronic back pain showed lower microstate D global explained variance, suggesting salience and attentional differences in clinical pain. Direct comparisons showed weaker pain-related increases in microstate C expression in both clinical back pain groups than capsaicin pain, with additional differences involving microstates A, D and E. These findings argue against a unitary EEG microstate signature of pain and instead reveal pain-type-specific patterns of large-scale brain dynamics, with microstate C providing the clearest distinction between experimental and clinical pain.

ai.topic: EEG Microstate Analysis Across Pain Conditions
ai.reason: Harmonized EEG microstate pipeline across conditions provides a reproducible framework for state classification and dynamical modeling, but clinical pain focus and human resting-state limits direct sleep/animal applicability.
ai.summary: Applied a harmonized EEG microstate analysis pipeline across three pain conditions—capsaicin-induced pain, non-chronic back pain, and chronic back pain—compared with matched controls or pain-free baseline. Found pain-type-specific microstate signatures: capsaicin pain increased microstate C expression and transitions toward C, non-chronic back pain showed lower microstate C occurrence, and chronic back pain showed lower microstate D global explained variance, arguing against a unitary microstate signature of pain.

papers.title: A Semi-Dry, Visually Comfortable c-VEP BCI with Short Calibration, Conservative Idle-State Behavior, and a VR Proof of Concept
papers.abstract: Background and Objectives: Code-modulated visual evoked potentials (c-VEPs) provide fast and reliable control signals for reactive brain-computer interfaces (rBCIs). However, deployment beyond laboratories remains limited by visually intrusive stimulation, reliance on wet electroencephalography (EEG), and false activations during non-control periods. We introduce a usability-oriented c-VEP rBCI combining low-salience textured stimulation, slow flashing codes, asynchronous evidence accumulation, and semi-dry EEG acquisition. Methods: Thirty participants evaluated the system on a standard screen using an 11-class keypad typing task. Two identical online typing sessions were separated by a 2-min video-viewing period serving as an explicit idle condition. Feasibility was then assessed in virtual reality (VR) through a proof-of-concept shell-game task involving head movements and immersive rendering constraints. Visual comfort, peripheral distraction, and fatigue were assessed subjectively in both conditions. Results: In the keypad task, the system achieved 99.8% accuracy with 33 s of calibration data and a mean decoding time of 4.3 s. No spurious commands occurred during the tested 2-min idle condition. In VR, online accuracy reached 100%, with a mean decoding time of 5.6 s. Participants reported high visual comfort and minimal peripheral distraction in both conditions, although fatigue was higher in VR. Conclusion: The proposed c-VEP rBCI combines short calibration, high accuracy, comfortable stimulation, semi-dry EEG, and asynchronous decision-making. Performance during the explicit idle condition and VR implementation support the feasibility of wearable and practical c-VEP systems for self-paced interaction beyond laboratory environments. These findings encourage evaluation in longer idle periods and real-world tasks.

ai.topic: Semi-Dry c-VEP BCI with Short Calibration
ai.reason: User calibration with small labeled data, asynchronous evidence accumulation, and semi-dry EEG acquisition are relevant for lightweight, user-friendly neurotechnology, though BCI application is outside sleep/animal focus.
ai.summary: Developed and evaluated a semi-dry, low-salience c-VEP brain-computer interface with slow flashing codes, asynchronous evidence accumulation, and conservative idle-state behavior in 30 participants. Achieved 99.8% accuracy with 33 s calibration and 4.3 s mean decoding in an 11-class keypad task, no spurious commands during a 2-min idle period, and 100% accuracy with 5.6 s decoding in a VR proof-of-concept, with high visual comfort but higher fatigue in VR.

papers.title: Dynamic Phase Synchrony in Cortical Networks Underlying Conscious Awareness of Flicker.
papers.abstract: Flickering light sources, such as fluorescent lamps, evoke neural oscillations in the occipital cortex aligning with the flicker frequency; however, this flicker often remains outside conscious awareness. This discrepancy suggests neural mechanisms gating flicker perception. While functional magnetic resonance imaging studies have indicated the involvement of large-scale frontal and parietal networks in conscious flicker perception, their low temporal resolution limits insights into the underlying dynamic interactions. Using electroencephalography and physically identical stimuli near the critical flicker-fusion frequency, we investigated the temporal dynamics of phase synchrony and power distribution. Flicker perception was characterized by an early increase in higher beta-band (19-28 Hz) synchrony, followed by an increase in gamma-band (29-48 Hz) synchrony between fronto-parietal and parieto-occipital regions at approximately 300 ms post-stimulus. This was accompanied by a global expansion of gamma-band power from occipital to fronto-parietal areas-effects not observed during fused perception. Conversely, alpha-band (8-14 Hz) synchrony between anterior and posterior regions showed a more pronounced reduction specifically during fusion. These findings suggest that frequency-specific coordination and global information sharing across large-scale networks may underlie conscious flicker perception. The emergence of broad gamma-band synchrony at around 300 ms may reflect the integration of local sensory signals into distributed cortical networks. Early beta-band synchrony may facilitate the initiation of this process through top-down modulation, whereas attenuated alpha-band synchrony during fusion may reflect insufficient engagement of these networks. Such dynamic interplay within distributed networks is suggested to be involved in shaping the temporal resolution of visual awareness.

ai.topic: Dynamic Phase Synchrony and Flicker Perception
ai.reason: EEG phase synchrony and time-frequency analysis of conscious perception; dynamic network methods are transferable to vigilance-state modeling, though not directly sleep or animal focused.
ai.summary: Using EEG near the critical flicker-fusion frequency, the study found that conscious flicker perception is characterized by early higher beta-band synchrony followed by gamma-band synchrony between fronto-parietal and parieto-occipital regions around 300 ms, alongside global gamma power expansion; fused perception showed stronger alpha-band synchrony reduction. These frequency-specific coordination patterns suggest a role for large-scale network dynamics in visual awareness.

papers.title: Spatial Sampling and Temporal Dynamics Shape Motor Decoding from Broadband Intracortical Signals
papers.abstract: Objective. Neural decoding performance depends strongly on neural signal representation; however, how the informative components of broadband intracortical activity vary with electrode configuration and decoding strategy remains unclear. We systematically compared the neural features spanning multiple temporal scales to identify the factors underlying robust motor decoding. Approach. Neural recordings were obtained from the dorsal premotor cortex, primary motor cortex, and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex of rhesus monkeys performing delayed-reaching tasks toward static or moving targets. Signals were recorded using 64-channel linear S-probes or 96-channel planar Utah arrays. We compared spiking-band power (SBP), local motor potential (LMP), and local field potential (LFP) power across multiple frequency bands using linear and nonlinear decoders. We further characterized the spectral and temporal components contributing to LMP decoding and evaluated the channel redundancy. Main results. The decoding performance of the SBP and high-frequency LFP features scaled with the number of recorded single units, whereas the LMP performance was more strongly influenced by the electrode geometry. LMP achieved a higher decoding performance with planar Utah arrays than with linear S-probes, accompanied by lower inter-electrode correlations and greater variability in preferred directions. Spectral analysis showed that LMP decoding was dominated by low-frequency components overlapping the delta band and movement-related cortical potentials, with an optimal decoding range of approximately 0.1-8 Hz. Nonlinear temporal decoders, particularly the convolutional neural network and gated recurrent unit models, further improved LMP decoding. Significance. These findings demonstrate that the neural features most informative for motor decoding depend on both the spatial sampling configuration and the temporal structure of the recorded activity. The results highlight the importance of low-frequency population dynamics and provide principles for optimizing neural-signal representations and reducing redundant neural data for scalable and wireless brain-computer interfaces.

ai.reason: Systematic comparison of neural features and decoders for motor decoding; valuable for signal representation and decoding strategies, but intracortical focus and motor task reduce direct relevance to EEG/EMG/ACC sleep research.
ai.summary: Comparing broadband intracortical signals in monkeys, the study found that spiking-band power and high-frequency LFP decoding scaled with single-unit count, whereas local motor potential decoding depended more on electrode geometry and performed better with planar Utah arrays; LMP decoding was dominated by low-frequency delta-band components (0.1–8 Hz). Nonlinear temporal decoders further improved LMP decoding, highlighting spatial sampling and temporal structure for motor brain-computer interfaces.

papers.title: EEG emotion recognition via multilevel entropy analysis: The power of entropy of entropy on phase dynamics.
papers.abstract: Emotion recognition from EEG signals has become a central task in affective computing, offering non-invasive insight into human emotional states. Due to the nonlinear and nonstationary nature of EEG, entropy-based features have gained prominence as reliable indicators of brain complexity. However, traditional entropy metrics-such as Shannon entropy (ShanEn) and its variants-often lack sensitivity to transient dynamics and multiscale irregularities in the brain's electrical activity. This study introduces a novel application of Entropy of Entropy (EoE) to EEG phase series (EoE - phase), aiming to enhance the detection of emotional states by capturing second-order variability in signal complexity. Unlike conventional measures, EoE quantifies not just signal unpredictability, but also the fluctuation of that unpredictability over time, offering a more dynamic representation of neural information flow. Using the GAMEEMO dataset, which includes EEG recordings from 28 participants during four emotion-evoking game scenarios (funny, boring, horror, calm), we computed and compared four feature sets: Phase Entropy, EoE - phase, ShanEn, and EoE applied to EEG amplitude time series. These features were classified using six machine learning models, including AdaBoost, SVM, and Random Forest. Our results demonstrate that EoE applied to phase dynamics significantly outperforms other entropy-based features, achieving a classification accuracy of 71.7% and AUC of 0.869 using the RF classifier with mixed PhaseEn and EoE-phase features, while traditional Shannon-based features reached only ~59% accuracy. This study provides the first systematic evaluation of EoE on EEG phase signals for emotion recognition, revealing its strong discriminative power and potential for integration into next-generation brain-computer interfaces.

ai.topic: Entropy-based EEG features for emotion recognition
ai.reason: Introduces multilevel entropy features (EoE) on EEG phase dynamics; the feature-engineering approach may be transferable to sleep/state classification, though the application is emotion recognition.
ai.summary: This study introduced Entropy of Entropy (EoE) applied to EEG phase series for emotion recognition, comparing it with phase entropy, Shannon entropy, and amplitude EoE on the GAMEEMO dataset. EoE-phase features significantly outperformed traditional entropy measures, achieving 71.7% accuracy and 0.869 AUC with a Random Forest classifier.

papers.title: EEG Signatures Support a Shrinking Spotlight of Attention After Errors.
papers.abstract: Errors inhibit attainment of our goals, but there are many ways to get back on track: from increased caution to heightened attention. In this report we examined EEG signatures of control and perception in 21 participants who completed a luminance-varying flanker task. Hierarchical Sequential Sample Modeling with a shrinking spotlight model was used for algorithmic decomposition of post-error adjustments. Control-related changes included a relationship between frontal midline theta power and raised decision threshold, as well as faster drift rate. Yet contrary to our hypothesis, these relationships were not significantly modulated following an error. Perceptual changes elicited by the luminance manipulation scaled with posterior alpha/beta power; both these extrinsic and intrinsic features loaded on an enhanced drift rate. Most importantly, after an error, this relationship between alpha/beta power and drift rate was enhanced. These findings support separate roles of neural systems in adaptive control: midfrontal regions were linked to generic control, whereas sensory-specific mechanisms of attentional adjustment were specifically recruited to boost evidence accumulation when control is needed.

ai.reason: Relevant EEG time-frequency analysis and hierarchical sequential modeling, with possible transfer of state-space/dynamical ideas to vigilance-state analyses, but focused on cognitive psychology rather than sleep or generalizable methods.
ai.summary: In a luminance-varying flanker task with EEG and hierarchical sequential sampling modeling, post-error adjustments involved frontal midline theta linked to increased decision threshold and faster drift rate, while posterior alpha/beta power scaled with drift rate and this relationship was enhanced after errors. The findings support separable roles of midfrontal control and sensory-specific attentional mechanisms in adaptive control.

papers.title: Evoked alpha oscillatory activity is suppressed by prolonged elbow pain and modulated by repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation.
papers.abstract: Alpha-band oscillatory activity, assessed using electroencephalography (EEG), is among the most widely studied neurophysiological markers of pain. However, the literature has focused predominantly on resting-state measures, leaving unclear whether pain also alters evoked alpha-band dynamics, measured via cortical perturbation using transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). Here, we examined whether prolonged pain alters TMS-evoked alpha event-related spectral perturbation (ERSP) and intertrial coherence (ITC), reflecting cortical reactivity and phase consistency, and whether 10-Hz repetitive TMS (rTMS) modulates these responses. We performed a secondary analysis on 2 previous experiments, which used nerve growth factor (NGF) injection to induce prolonged elbow muscle pain. In experiment 1, participants underwent primary motor cortex (M1) TMS-EEG at baseline (day 0) pre-NGF injection and day 2 (peak pain) and day 7 (pain resolution) post-injection. In experiment 2, M1-TMS-EEG was assessed on day 0 before NGF injection and again on day 4 after injection, with active or sham 10-Hz rTMS delivered to M1 between these assessments. In experiment 1, M1 TMS-EEG showed reductions in alpha ERSP (P = 0.014) and alpha ITC (P = 0.041) from day 0 to day 2. In experiment 2, active rTMS produced a more positive pre-to-post change in alpha ERSP (P = 0.006) relative to sham but did not alter alpha ITC (P = 0.804). Our findings suggest that prolonged experimental pain is associated with diminished evoked alpha oscillatory activity, whereas high-frequency rTMS modulates this activity in the positive direction. These findings suggest that perturbation-evoked alpha metrics warrant further investigation as candidate biomarkers of pain state and response to neuromodulation.

ai.reason: Evoked alpha oscillatory analysis using time-frequency methods is methodologically relevant, but clinical pain/TMS focus and secondary analysis reduce direct applicability to sleep or animal experiments.
ai.summary: In secondary analyses of two experiments using nerve growth factor-induced prolonged elbow pain, TMS-EEG showed reduced alpha event-related spectral perturbation and intertrial coherence at peak pain compared with baseline, and active 10-Hz rTMS increased alpha ERSP relative to sham without altering ITC. The results suggest evoked alpha activity as a candidate marker of pain state and neuromodulation response.

papers.title: Repetitive negative thinking is associated with conflict-related neural activity that modulates evidence accumulation.
papers.abstract: Repetitive negative thinking (RNT), including worry and rumination, is a transdiagnostic feature of anxiety and depressive disorders and is linked to altered cognitive control. However, the decision-level mechanisms underlying these alterations are not well understood. Here, we examined whether individual variation in RNT is associated with neural and computational markers of conflict processing. Thirty-seven participants completed a flanker task while undergoing electroencephalography, and inhibitory control dynamics were quantified using hierarchical drift diffusion modeling. Behaviorally, RNT was not associated with traditional behavioral markers of conflict processing. At the neural level, higher RNT was associated with a more negative midfrontal conflict N2. Computationally, higher RNT was associated with larger congruent-incongruent differences in drift rate. Similarly, more negative midfrontal N2 activity was associated with greater modulation of drift rate congruency effects. An exploratory mediation analysis indicated that the midfrontal conflict N2 significantly mediated the effect of RNT on drift rate differences between congruent and incongruent trials. These findings indicate that elevated RNT is associated with heightened conflict-related neural activity that increases the degree to which evidence accumulation is modulated by conflict, suggesting a more reactive and context-sensitive engagement of cognitive control.
papers.journal: Journal of mood and anxiety disorders

ai.reason: Uses EEG and hierarchical drift diffusion modeling to study cognitive control; computational modeling is transferable but psychological focus and lack of sleep/animal relevance limit utility.
ai.summary: In 37 participants completing a flanker task with EEG and hierarchical drift diffusion modeling, higher repetitive negative thinking was associated with a more negative midfrontal conflict N2 and larger congruent-incongruent drift-rate differences, and the N2 mediated the relationship between RNT and drift-rate modulation. The findings link RNT to heightened conflict-related neural activity that increases context-sensitive evidence accumulation.

papers.title: Effective connectivity in the active encoding of facial emotions: a dynamic causal modeling study.
papers.abstract: Previous studies have identified brain regions involved in the active encoding of emotional content of facial expressions (ECFEs); however, little is known about how these regions interact within a functional network. Electroencephalography data were recorded from 62 healthy university students performing a delayed match-to-sample task in which facial expressions served as both encoding and interfering stimuli. Dynamic causal modeling was applied to examine encoding-related modulations of effective connectivity among six nodes in bilateral inferior occipital, inferior temporal, and inferior frontal gyri. During the early time window (1-200 ms), encoding modulated almost all the connectivities including reduced bottom-up excitatory and strengthened top-down inhibitory visual-temporal connectivities, strengthened bidirectional visual-frontal connectivities, and reduced bidirectional temporal-frontal connectivities. During the later window (200-400 ms), only a subset of connectivities was modulated, marked by strengthened top-down excitatory and inhibitory connectivities from frontal and temporal regions to visual areas. Modulation strength was not reliably associated with behavioral performance. Exploratory Bayesian model selection within a restricted model space showed a numerical advantage for a bottom-up excitatory model during encoding and a top-down excitatory model during interference suppression under fixed-effects modeling; however, random-effects analysis indicated that this preference was modest and not uniform across participants. These findings suggest that the active encoding of ECFEs is supported, but not determined, by directional interactions among brain modules, implicating strengthened high-order top-down control over posterior sensory areas, together with functional decoupling of face-sensitive areas from ongoing visual input.

ai.topic: Dynamic causal modeling of effective connectivity in facial emotion encoding
ai.reason: Applies DCM to EEG data, relevant to dynamical-system modeling of neural time series, but the specific cognitive task and connectivity focus are adjacent to sleep/EEG methods.
ai.summary: Using dynamic causal modeling on EEG data from 62 participants performing a delayed match-to-sample task with facial emotions, this study examined effective connectivity among six nodes in bilateral occipital, temporal, and frontal regions during encoding. Results showed early encoding modulated widespread connectivities including reduced bottom-up excitation and strengthened top-down inhibition, while later encoding involved a subset of top-down effects, with modulation strength not reliably linked to behavior.

papers.title: Beyond processed depth targets: frontal EEG patterns, brain vulnerability, and postoperative delirium in older adults.
papers.abstract: Limited-channel frontal electroencephalography is widely used during anesthesia through processed EEG platforms, but clinical interpretation often remains centered on numerical depth indices. This narrative review examines whether frontal EEG signals, including raw waveforms, suppression behavior, spectral features, and processed index behavior, may provide information beyond hypnotic depth in older adults at risk for postoperative delirium. A targeted literature search was performed in PubMed/MEDLINE and Google Scholar for articles published from database inception through April 30, 2026. Priority was given to randomized trials, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, consensus statements, prospective observational studies, and mechanistic studies relevant to processed EEG monitoring, frontal EEG interpretation, postoperative delirium, aging, frailty, anesthesia, and critical care. Evidence from randomized trials and systematic reviews suggests that processed EEG-guided anesthetic titration and suppression minimization alone do not reliably prevent postoperative delirium. However, several clinically accessible frontal EEG patterns may provide contextual information about anesthetic sensitivity and reduced cerebral reserve. These include reduced frontal alpha power, early or disproportionate burst suppression, spectral slowing or low spectral edge frequency, and disorganized emergence. Their interpretation depends on anesthetic dose and agent, hemodynamics, signal quality, artifact burden, frailty, baseline cognition, and postoperative recovery context. Limited-channel frontal EEG should be interpreted as a contextual brain-monitoring signal rather than a single-number depth target. Future studies should test whether multimodal frameworks integrating frontal EEG patterns with physiologic and patient-level variables improve postoperative neurocognitive outcomes.
papers.journal: Journal of clinical monitoring and computing

ai.topic: Frontal EEG and postoperative delirium in older adults
ai.reason: Narrative review on clinical EEG monitoring for delirium; only adjacent to computational methods and not directly transferable to animal sleep analysis.
ai.summary: This narrative review examined whether frontal EEG signals beyond processed depth indices provide information about postoperative delirium risk in older adults, synthesizing evidence from randomized trials, systematic reviews, and observational studies. It concluded that processed EEG-guided titration alone does not reliably prevent delirium, but patterns such as reduced alpha power, burst suppression, and spectral slowing may reflect anesthetic sensitivity and reduced cerebral reserve, supporting contextual interpretation.

papers.title: Transdiagnostic patterns of electroencephalography (EEG)-derived aperiodic activity across schizophrenia-spectrum, bipolar, and depressive disorders: A systematic review.
papers.abstract: Aperiodic electroencephalographic activity is proposed as a scalable marker of cortical population dynamics relevant to excitation-inhibition balance. However, it remains unclear whether aperiodic parameters represent disorder-specific abnormalities or context-sensitive indices of clinically relevant brain states. Consistent with systematic-review guidelines and a prospectively registered protocol, Ovid databases and PubMed were searched from inception through February 9, 2026, with updated manual searching conducted through July 14, 2026. Peer-reviewed studies reporting electroencephalography-derived aperiodic parameters in adults with schizophrenia-spectrum disorders, major depressive disorder, treatment-resistant depression, and/or bipolar disorder were eligible. Studies lacking aperiodic outcomes or separable findings for eligible diagnoses were excluded. Two reviewers independently conducted study screening, data extraction, and risk-of-bias assessments. Findings were synthesized narratively by diagnosis, recording context, and parameter. Thirty articles (N = 2298 aggregate participants) spanning cross-sectional, longitudinal, and interventional designs were included. Findings in schizophrenia-spectrum disorders were heterogeneous, with several studies reporting steeper slopes, higher offsets, or reduced temporal flexibility relative to healthy controls. Task-related and dynamic measures often showed greater clinical relevance than static resting-state parameters. Studies of major depressive disorder and treatment-resistant depression more consistently reported flatter slopes and reduced offsets, particularly in central and posterior regions, with evidence from sleep and intracranial recordings. Aperiodic parameters were sensitive to treatment-related modulation, although the direction of change differed across interventions. Bipolar disorder evidence was limited, and methodological heterogeneity precluded quantitative synthesis. Aperiodic electroencephalographic activity may be more informative as a context-sensitive, within-subject marker of cortical state and treatment-related change than a fixed diagnostic signature. Methodological harmonization and direct physiological validation remain necessary before clinical implementation.
keywords: schizophrenia spectrum and other psychotic disorders

ai.topic: Aperiodic EEG activity in psychiatric disorders
ai.reason: Aperiodic activity is a transferable EEG feature for sleep/vigilance analysis, and the systematic review touches on methodological aspects like recording context and parameters, but focuses on clinical psychiatric applications rather than computational methods or animal sleep.
ai.summary: This systematic review synthesized 30 peer-reviewed studies (N=2298) on EEG-derived aperiodic activity in schizophrenia-spectrum, bipolar, and depressive disorders. It found heterogeneous results in schizophrenia-spectrum disorders (steeper slopes, higher offsets, reduced temporal flexibility), flatter slopes and reduced offsets in major depressive and treatment-resistant depression (especially central/posterior), limited bipolar evidence, and treatment sensitivity, suggesting aperiodic parameters may be more useful as context-sensitive within-subject markers than fixed diagnostic signatures.

papers.title: Optimization of visibility-adaptive expressway early warning schemes under sand-dust weather considering driver workload.
papers.abstract: Objective: Sand-dust weather conditions severely reduce visibility and pavement friction on desert expressways, substantially increasing crash risks. Existing early warning systems rely primarily on fixed thresholds and single-modal information, often neglecting driver cognitive and physiological workload. This study aimed to develop and optimize a visibility-adaptive multimodal early warning scheme for desert expressways under sand-dust weather conditions, with a focus on balancing driving safety and human workload.Methods: A high-fidelity driving simulator was used to construct four visibility scenarios: 500, 300, 100, and 50 m, representing typical sand-dust weather conditions on the Wuma Expressway. Thirty-six licensed drivers completed 64 orthogonal test conditions combining variable message signs (VMS), LED linear guidance, and voice navigation. Eye movement, driving behavior, and physiological indices (ECG and EEG) were synchronously collected. ACriteria Importance Through Intercriteria Correlation (CRITIC)-weighted multidimensional evaluation system was established, incorporating speed compliance, steering stability, heart rate (HR), and EEG β/θ ratio, to screen the optimal scheme via Euclidean distance decision-making.Results: Visibility significantly deteriorated driving performance and elevated workload. The optimal multimodal schemes varied by visibility: 500 m (60 flashes/min LEDs + speed/distance voice); 300-100 m (120 flashes/min LEDs + steering/fog-light voice); 50 m (constant LEDs + operational guidance). Compared with single-modal warnings, the optimized scheme demonstrated statistically significant improvements at 500 m and 300 m visibility (p < 0.0031, Bonferroni-corrected), increasing speed compliance by 10.6 percentage points (to 89.2%), reducing steering angle deviation by 0.005-0.01 rad and lateral acceleration deviation by 0.05-0.1 m/s2, lowering heart rate by 4.28 bpm, and raising the β/θ ratio by 0.14. At 100 m and 50 m visibility, nonsignificant but directionally consistent trends were observed (p = 0.011 and p = 0.034, respectively; Cohen's d = 0.43 and 0.37), indicating a practical reduction in overall physiological load of approximately 15-20% that warrants further validation under stringent statistical thresholds.Conclusions: The visibility-adaptive multimodal early warning scheme effectively improves driving stability and mitigates driver workload under sand-dust weather conditions. Tiered information delivery and dynamic LED parameters enhance information perception and reduce visual fatigue. The findings offer a cognitive-load-informed framework to guide the parameter tuning of traffic management strategies and safety improvement on desert expressways during extreme sand-dust weather.

papers.title: Desflurane Increases Hippocampal RAF-MAPK-MSK1 Protein Levels and Reduces CLOCK Expression: Sorafenib Attenuates Cognitive Impairment in Aged Mice.
papers.abstract: Postoperative cognitive dysfunction (POCD) is common after anesthesia and surgery in older adults, yet no targeted therapy exists, and the mechanism linking volatile anesthetic exposure to circadian dysregulation in the aged hippocampus is undefined. Here we show that RAF manipulation bidirectionally alters CLOCK protein levels in HT22 hippocampal neurons, and that RAF-MAPK-MSK1 protein abundance is inversely related to CLOCK levels in the aged hippocampus after desflurane exposure. Aged C57BL/6 mice (18 months, both sexes) were exposed to 2% desflurane for 2 h, with or without pretreatment with the multi-kinase RAF inhibitor sorafenib (50 mg/kg), and phenotypes were assessed by Western blot, immunofluorescence, in vivo electroencephalography, whole-cell patch-clamp recordings of CA1 pyramidal neurons, and behavioral testing (righting reflex, contextual fear conditioning, Morris water maze). Parallel dissection in HT22 hippocampal neurons employed RAF knockdown, overexpression, and pharmacological inhibition. Desflurane increased total c-Raf, ERK1/2 (MAPK), and MSK1 protein levels-phosphorylation status was not assessed-while reducing CLOCK in both HT22 cells and aged hippocampus, accompanied by cellular senescence, impaired S-phase entry, increased hippocampal β-galactosidase and α-synuclein immunoreactivity, synaptic excitation-inhibition imbalance, and deficits in contextual fear memory and spatial learning. In HT22 cells, RAF knockdown normalized kinase abundance and restored CLOCK, whereas overexpression exacerbated these changes. In aged mice, sorafenib restored CLOCK, attenuated hippocampal β-galactosidase and α-synuclein immunoreactivity, and improved cognitive performance. These findings support a link between RAF-MAPK-MSK1 protein abundance and hippocampal CLOCK in desflurane-induced cognitive impairment and nominate RAF inhibition as a candidate strategy warranting further preclinical study.

papers.title: Respiration and individual differences shape behavioral and inter-brain synchronization
papers.abstract: Humans coordinate their actions while their bodies and brains synchronize in social interactions, yet how behavioral, physiological, and neural dynamics interact during interpersonal coordination remains largely unknown. We investigated how respiration and individual differences influence behavioral and inter-brain synchrony in a musical synchronization task, which requires precise temporal alignment. Eighty-eight individuals first produced a familiar melody at their most comfortable rate to measure their spontaneous production rate (SPR). They then synchronized the melody with a randomly assigned unfamiliar partner under natural (unpaced), instructed in-phase, and instructed anti-phase breathing conditions, while hyperscanning 64-channel electroencephalography (EEG), respiration, auditory-motor timing, and perceived social connectedness were recorded. Relative to natural respiration, both in-phase and anti-phase breathing increased inter-brain phase-locking and perceived social closeness but reduced behavioral synchrony; the instructed respiratory phase relationship was mirrored in their inter-brain relative phase. Differences in phase of respiratory cycles (inhalation and exhalation) also influenced coordination: Inhalation was associated with stronger inter-brain synchronization but less precise and stable behavioral coordination than was exhalation. Moreover, Individual differences influenced coordination: Partners with the faster SPR consistently preceded the slower partners and exhibited an alpha-band inter-brain phase advance in synchronization, whereas dyads with similar SPR showed greater behavioral synchrony and smaller inter-brain phase difference. Our findings identify respiration as a previously overlooked factor that organizes behavioral and neural synchronization, while individual intrinsic rhythms constrain how interacting partners align in time. Together, these findings reveal a dynamic interplay between the rhythms of the body and brain during human social interactions.

papers.title: When the Electromyography (EMG) and the Patient Disagree: Unraveling a Motor Neuron Disease Mimic With Small-Fiber Dysfunction.
papers.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by upper and lower motor neuron dysfunction. Electromyography (EMG) is central to its evaluation, but neurogenic abnormalities and fasciculations are not specific to ALS and must be interpreted within the clinical phenotype and disease trajectory. This study reports a 52-year-old man with an approximately eight-year history of intermittent muscle twitching, bilateral upper-limb tremor, muscular tightness and warmth, and asymmetric cutaneous hypersensitivity. An initial electrodiagnostic evaluation raised concern for diffuse motor neuron disease, despite preserved strength, normal gait, absence of muscle wasting, and lack of clear upper motor neuron signs. Extensive evaluation for inflammatory, autoimmune, metabolic, toxic, infectious, paraneoplastic, neuromuscular junction, and peripheral nerve hyperexcitability disorders was unrevealing. Serum creatine kinase was mildly and variably elevated, while aldolase and a comprehensive myositis panel were normal. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated no supportive features of ALS. Sudomotor testing showed reduced electrochemical skin conductance (ESC) in the hands, supporting small-fiber/autonomic dysfunction in the context of prominent sensory symptoms. Repeat EMG, performed after interval follow-up with broad muscle sampling, demonstrated focal neurogenic abnormalities involving bilateral ulnar distributions and left L5-S1 radiculopathy but found no electrophysiological evidence of a neurodegenerative disorder. The patient was treated symptomatically with gabapentin and vitamin E and reported approximately 80% improvement after six weeks. This case highlights the importance of clinicophysiological correlation, disease trajectory, sensory phenomenology, and repeat electrophysiology when an initial EMG suggests motor neuron disease but the longitudinal clinical picture is discordant. It also illustrates how small-fiber dysfunction and focal neurogenic abnormalities may coexist and mimic a progressive motor neuron syndrome.

papers.title: Positive interactions and active mentalizing facilitate inter-brain synchronization in couples.
papers.abstract: High-quality interactions rely on socio-cognitive abilities, which help partners understand and respond to one another. Hyperscanning, which measures brain activity in multiple individuals simultaneously, can examine inter-brain synchronization as a possible signature of social coordination. In this study, we explore this synchronization during natural, everyday interactions in romantic couples. Forty-two dyads participated in a naturalistic behavioral paradigm while EEG was recorded. We measured behavioral dyadic reciprocity and negative states, and computed inter-brain synchronization using the circular correlation coefficient (CCorr) across multiple frequency bands (Theta [4-8 Hz], Alpha [8-13 Hz], and Beta [14-31 Hz]). Positive interactions elicited greater dyadic reciprocity and fewer negative states compared to negative interactions. At the neural level, inter-brain synchronization in the beta band was significantly higher during positive compared to negative interactions. Mentalizing compared to counting elicited increased inter-brain synchronization in both alpha and beta bands, indicating that active sociocognitive processing enhances neural alignment between partners. These findings demonstrate that inter-brain dynamics provide a neural signature of both interaction valence and mentalizing engagement during real-world social interactions, putting forward inter-brain synchronization as a sensitive marker of sociocognitive coordination.

Mentalizing versus counting increased alpha- and beta-band synchronization, supporting inter-brain synchronization as a marker of interaction valence and sociocognitive engagement.

papers.title: Quantitative assessment of cervical spinal cord injury: Methods, clinical utility, and future directions.
papers.abstract: Literature review. To provide a structured narrative summary of quantitative assessment methods for cervical spinal cord injury (SCI), analyze their stage-specific applicability, discuss limitations, and clarify the clinical utility and future integration of wearable sensors and artificial intelligence (AI). A narrative review was conducted using PubMed, Web of Science, and EBSCO to identify English-language, peer-reviewed studies published between 1967 and 2026 on quantitative assessment of traumatic and non-traumatic cervical SCI. The search covered imaging, neurological and functional evaluation, electrophysiology, biomechanics, wearable monitoring, artificial intelligence, machine learning, computer vision, and multimodal data integration. An updated PubMed search performed on May 15, 2026 identified 1,042 records. After title and abstract screening, 873 records were retained as potentially relevant, and 73 unique publications were included in the final narrative synthesis following full-text review and deduplication. Main methods include imaging (CT, MRI/DTI, AI-image analysis), neurological scales (ASIA/ISNCSCI, SCIM, WISCI), neuroelectrophysiology (SSEP, MEP, EMG), biomechanics (sEMG and kinematics), and wearable sensors. These methods provide complementary structural, neurological, functional, and real-world activity information across acute care, rehabilitation, and long-term follow-up. Current approaches remain limited by subjectivity, poor real-time monitoring, limited quantification precision, equipment dependence, and insensitivity to early or subclinical changes. Wearable-AI integration may improve continuous monitoring, risk prediction, pressure injury prevention, and the selection of patients who may benefit from transcutaneous or epidural stimulation. Current quantitative assessment methods for cervical SCI are insufficient when used alone. A staged, multimodal strategy that combines conventional clinical assessment with wearable sensing and AI-supported analysis may improve full-process management, clinical decision-making, and prognostic assessment in cervical SCI.

papers.title: A neuroeducational approach to STEM education: Integrating real-time cognitive analysis and cognitive load theory to optimize teaching and learning at universities.
papers.abstract: The relevance of science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) education to effectively meet challenging academic requirements has become imperative for university entrants. With emerging advancements within the domain of learning neuroscience and analytics, it has become possible to analyze and track the real-time mental states of learners. This has opened several avenues to apply the theoretical perspectives of Cognitive Load Theory (CLT). Though applications of neuro-technological interventions for learning have become widely sought, their effective implementation within STEM education has not been comprehensive at the university level. The innovations brought about within this study include its conceptual fusion for STEM education based upon real-time mental state analysis and CLT. The goal of this research is to integrate the current research findings on real-time cognitive analysis practices used in STEM education in universities and analyze how cognitive load can be monitored dynamically and discuss teaching practices according to principles of CLT to improve effectiveness and inclusiveness for better cognitive load management throughout learning. A systematic narrative review with cross-case synthesis was conducted using peer-reviewed empirical studies published between 2018 and 2025. The relevant articles were identified through the searching of databases such as Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC, and PsycINFO. Studies focusing on higher education STEM contexts were included if they employed neuroeducational tools (e.g., electroencephalography, functional near-infrared spectroscopy, eye tracking, or artificial intelligence-driven analytics) or incorporated instructional designs informed by Cognitive Load Theory (CLT). A standardized framework for extracting data was used, and data were thematically analyzed to identify patterns across the studies regarding cognitive load measurement, adaptive instructional strategies, learning outcomes, teacher experiences, and ethical considerations. From the synthesis, real-time cognitive feedback is perceived to have positively influenced teaching effectiveness by allowing the instructor to dynamically adjust pacing, scaffolding, and learning activities (d = 0.68-0.72, P < 0.01). Multimodal cognitive analytics were also associated with more precise estimates of cognitive load, supporting the development of adaptive learning strategies. It is also apparent that cognitively based personalization is effective in reducing the cognitive load and improving motivation and knowledge acquisition for both diverse and neurodiverse students. The synergistic combination of real-time cognitive analysis and CLT has the potential for making progressive inroads for inclusive and adaptive STEM education in universities. This conceptual combination is in good harmony with the benchmarks for health and educational policy that regard evidence-based instruction, the welfare of the learner, and equity in higher educational settings as cornerstones. Longitudinal study, ethical regulation, and implementation strategies for neuroeducational data in universities need more emphasis in future studies.

papers.title: Increased encoding of aversive stimuli by lateral habenula neurons during Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol withdrawal.
papers.abstract: The lateral habenula (LHb) integrates cortical and basal forebrain (BF) input and is implicated in negative affective states, but its involvement in negative affect associated with cannabis withdrawal is unknown. Here, effects of withdrawal from the psychoactive cannabis constituent, Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol (Δ9-THC), on fear conditioning (FC) and LHb function were measured in rats using calcium photometry and electrophysiology. FC-associated LHb calcium signals, freezing behavior, and LHb excitatory-inhibitory (E-I) ratios were increased during Δ9-THC withdrawal, and local GABA release was impaired, indicating disinhibition of LHb output neurons. GABA release was also impaired at optogenetically activated BF-LHb axons, and not from ventral tegmental area-LHb inputs. The results indicate that Δ9-THC withdrawal increases LHb excitability through disinhibition, contributing to increased fear of primary and conditioned aversive stimuli. Our findings implicate the LHb in cannabis withdrawal-associated negative affect and offer insight into the neural mechanisms of cannabis use disorder.

papers.title: Boder's dyslexia subtypes as a severity continuum with a definitional route axis - A behavioural companion to harmonised qEEG cross-spectra.
papers.abstract: Developmental dyslexia is classically divided into Boder's dysphonetic (DD), dyseidetic (DYD) and mixed (MD) subtypes, assigned by direct reading-and-spelling testing. Its computerised Italian adaptation, the Direct Test of Reading and Spelling (DTRS), assigns the subtype algorithmically from the reading quotient and the percentage of correctly spelt known and unknown words. Using the same source clinical cohort and the same stable and sparse regression classifier (SSRC) as our companion, we asked whether the subtypes form natural clusters or lie on a continuum, and whether reading-time (severity) or qualitative-error (route) information discriminates them. We analysed one DTRS assessment each from 520 children (378 DD, 41 DYD, 101 MD), deriving reading-time indices, including a severity/fluency index (SFI), and Boder's error taxonomies for reading and spelling. Subtype structure was probed with Gaussian-mixture clustering (adjusted Rand index against clinical labels) and Hartigan's dip test; discrimination with the SSRC and robust ROC under participant-level Monte-Carlo cross-validation, with subsampling stability intervals (5th-95th percentile over 300 iterations). Full-sample pairwise AUCs were additionally evaluated with percentile bootstrap 95% confidence intervals (10,000 subject-level resamples of the full-sample classifier scores) and label-permutation tests (10,000 permutations, one-sided and Bonferroni-corrected within each model). No feature space yielded label-aligned mixture solutions (adjusted Rand index ≈ 0); SFI was unimodal (dip p = 0.36). Reading-time indices separated the severity contrast (DD vs MD, stable AUC 0.73 [0.66-0.80]; p < 0.001) but were weak and non-significant for the route contrast (DYD vs DD, 0.58 [0.47-0.69]; p = 0.543, non-significant); reading qualitative errors showed a weak route signal (0.61 [0.50-0.73]; p = 0.062) that did not reach Bonferroni-corrected significance. Unknown-word spelling, the basis of the diagnostic algorithm, separated DD from DYD almost perfectly (0.94-0.98), but partialling out unknown-word accuracy collapsed this to 0.60: the separation is definitional. The severity contrast was likewise definitional: the reading quotient alone separated DD from MD at 0.86, and residualising the reading-time indices on the reading quotient within each training fold reduced the DD-MD AUC from 0.73 to 0.50. In the EEG subsample, no behavioural classifier separated DD from DYD significantly (TIME: 0.52 [0.31-0.75], p = 0.41; ERR: weak and non-significant 0.62 [0.41-0.81], p = 0.15), whereas qEEG cross-spectral connectivity did so at 0.85 in the published qEEG sample of 227 children (169 DD, 18 DYD, 40 MD; Chiarenza et al., 2026). No evidence for natural clusters emerged with the present methods: the subtypes behave as overlapping regions of graded continuous distributions. Both axes of Boder's scheme are threshold-defined - severity by the reading quotient, route by unknown-word spelling - and both are continuously distributed. Once the defining variable is removed, reading dynamics carry no residual severity signal (0.50) and independent behaviour carries only a faint route signal (0.58-0.61); the route distinction is clearest in brain connectivity, which predicts the behaviourally defined labels rather than independently validating a latent route construct. Together, the two papers advance a dimensional, mechanism-aware account of dyslexia subtyping.

papers.title: SPORADIC CREUTZFELDT-JAKOB DISEASE: CLINICAL FEATURES, DIAGNOSIS AND THERAPEUTIC HORIZONS.
papers.abstract: Sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (sCJD) is a rare, rapidly progressive, and fatal prion disease that remains a major diagnostic and therapeutic challenge. Its presentation often overlaps with other causes of rapidly progressive dementia, making early recognition essential, particularly to exclude potentially reversible conditions. This review provides an updated overview of the diagnostic tools, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) biomarkers, prognostic factors, clinical progression, differential diagnosis, and current management strategies in sCJD. A literature-based review was conducted using PubMed and Scopus for articles published between October 1, 2015, and October 1, 2025, focusing on patients with suspected or confirmed CJD. Clinical features, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), electroencephalography (EEG), CSF biomarkers, prognostic indicators, and therapeutic approaches were synthesized. Current diagnosis of sCJD relies on the integration of clinical presentation with MRI, EEG, and CSF testing. Diffusion-weighted MRI and real-time quaking-induced conversion (RT-QuIC) have substantially improved antemortem diagnostic accuracy, while traditional biomarkers such as 14-3-3 protein and total tau remain useful supportive tests. Prognosis is uniformly poor, with median survival usually limited to a few months, although disease course varies according to age, PRNP codon 129 polymorphism, and molecular subtype. Important differential diagnoses include autoimmune encephalitis, viral encephalitis, vascular cognitive impairment, and other neurodegenerative disorders presenting with rapidly progressive dementia. No disease-modifying therapy has shown definitive benefit, and management remains primarily supportive and symptom-directed. Advances in biomarkers and greater understanding of molecular heterogeneity may improve early diagnosis, prognostication, and future therapeutic development.

papers.title: PIP2 binding at allosteric site blocks activation in human rod CNG channels.
papers.abstract: Phosphatidylinositol-4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) is a signaling lipid that regulates multiple ion channels. In rod cyclic nucleotide-gated (CNG) channels, PIP2 was reported to inhibit activity, controlling light sensitivity and dynamic range. Reports of low PIP2 levels in rod outer segment (ROS) membranes questioned the physiological relevance of such inhibition, and the underlying mechanism remained unclear. Here we define the mechanism of PIP2 inhibition of human CNGA1, the principal rod CNG channel subunit. Flux assays and single-channel electrophysiology of purified, liposome-reconstituted CNGA1 channels demonstrate inhibition at PIP2 concentrations estimated for ROS membranes. Cryo-EM structures of PIP2-free channels in lipid nanodiscs capture closed, intermediate, and open conformations, whereas the open state is absent with PIP2. PIP2 binds at the interface between voltage-sensing, pore, and C-linker domains, stabilizing closed states and sterically preventing channel opening. Our findings establish the physiological relevance and structural mechanism of PIP2 inhibition, and provide an inhibitory allosteric site for therapeutic targeting.

papers.title: Isolated Aphasia as an Epileptic Manifestation of Neurosarcoidosis: A Case Report.
papers.abstract: Acute aphasia requires urgent evaluation for stroke, but recurrent and stereotyped language disturbances may also reflect focal seizures. We report the case of a 23-year-old man brought to the emergency department (ED) with aphasia that had been present for approximately six hours. Over the preceding week, he had experienced several similar but briefer episodes that had resolved spontaneously. He was concurrently undergoing investigation at another institution for persistent hiccups and near-daily vomiting of more than one month's duration. Chest computed tomography (CT) and positron emission tomography (PET)-computed tomography had already shown mediastinal and mesenteric lymphadenopathy suggestive of sarcoidosis, although other etiologies, including malignancy, could not be excluded. Neurological examination was limited by the language disturbance but showed no obvious motor deficit. Brain computed tomography revealed obstructive hydrocephalus with transependymal cerebrospinal fluid flow and multiple enhancing nodular lesions, predominantly in and around the ventricular system. Electroencephalography demonstrated epileptiform activity, and the aphasia resolved after treatment with levetiracetam and clobazam. Further cerebrospinal fluid analysis, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and pathological investigations supported a diagnosis of probable neurosarcoidosis presenting with lymphocytic meningoencephalitis and obstructive hydrocephalus. This case illustrates an unusual pathophysiological sequence, isolated aphasia as a focal epileptic manifestation of neurosarcoidosis, and is a reminder that unexplained focal neurological symptoms, particularly when fluctuating or recurrent, warrant the consideration of seizures and early electroencephalography.
